sources.title: MobileWAM: Bridging World Action Models to Mobile Manipulation with Chain-of-Foresight

sectionsRead: 4.2 Comparison with the State of the Art
C Real-Robot System and Task Suite
E Mobile MoE Expert Routing Analysis
omissions: All supplied main text and appendix text were read. Figure captions were read, but figure images were not inspected.
Tables were inspected through the supplied text; original PDF layout was not visually checked.
Supplementary videos and any separate supplements were not supplied or inspected.
Code was not inspected and experiments were not reproduced.

The identifier, title and all 17 catalog authors match the supplied title page. It labels the artifact arXiv:2608.04657v2, dated 6 August 2026, while the document date is August 7, 2026; no revision history was supplied to resolve that date difference.
Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.

synopsis: MobileWAM trains a video-derived representation for whole-body mobile control, then deploys it without generating futures. Its distinctive additions are a recurrent future-latent supervision branch and soft mixtures of locomotion, manipulation and shared action experts. Reported evidence includes 73.0% mean simulated subtask success and improvements over π0.5 on five physical tasks. However, inconsistent state-input descriptions and limited evaluation reporting qualify the claims of unprivileged sensing and long-horizon generalization. [E03–E06, E10, E16, E18]

problem.text: The authors argue that mobile manipulation requires representations that handle camera ego-motion, multiple feasible base–arm trajectories, and navigation errors whose consequences appear during later manipulation. They seek to transfer video-model dynamics priors into coordinated control without paying for future-video generation during deployment.

contributions.text: A pretrained video transformer and a smaller action transformer interact through layerwise attention, with an asymmetric mask permitting cached current-observation features during action generation.
Chain-of-Foresight supplies recurrent future-latent supervision, while a three-expert feed-forward mixture provides soft specialization within the action pathway.
Component ablations connect these additions to improved executed simulation success; physical experiments establish limited transfer on randomized initial conditions within the training distribution.

inputs: Current head and wrist RGB images, composited side by side at 384 × 640 resolution.
A language instruction encoded by a frozen T5-family encoder.
Robot-state conditioning; its definition differs between Section 3.1 and Appendix A.
Training only: demonstration action chunks and future video latents.
outputs: Deployment: a four-step chunk of 13-dimensional whole-body commands.
Training: action and future-video velocity estimates, plus auxiliary foresight velocity estimates and beliefs.

steps.name: Encode the present
steps.detail: A frozen 3D VAE compresses the paired-camera video by 16 spatially and 4 temporally. The current observation remains clean; future training latents receive noise. The world transformer has 30 blocks of width 3072. One visual latent tick aligns with one four-action chunk.

steps.name: Denoise coordinated actions
steps.detail: A separate 30-block action transformer of width 1024 joins visual tokens through shared attention at every layer, using separate projections. The 13 command dimensions cover seven arm joints, gripper, head pan/tilt, torso lift and base linear/angular velocities. State conditioning enters the cross-attention context.

steps.name: Mix motion experts
steps.detail: Every action feed-forward layer contains three cloned experts. A zero-initialized linear router reads mean-pooled noisy-action embeddings and produces temperature-1 softmax weights. Their outputs are combined densely; expert names describe intended specialization rather than hard assignments to command dimensions.

steps.name: Train a chain of future beliefs
steps.detail: A two-layer MLP fuses current-observation features from backbone layers 4, 12, 20 and 30. Three independently parameterized foresight modules sequentially receive the preceding belief and a noised future latent. Each contains three backbone-width transformer blocks and predicts both a flow velocity and the next belief. Gradients propagate through the entire chain into the backbone.

training.text: Benchmark adaptation jointly fine-tunes both transformer experts in one stage, keeping the VAE and text encoder frozen. AdamW uses learning rate 10^-5, batch size 256, cosine decay, 5% warmup and bf16. The principal objective weights video and action equally, with CoF coefficient 0.1 and depth weights (0.4, 0.2, 0.1).

Video and action use independently sampled noise levels. CoF uses noise-schedule shift 10, compared with 5 for the main branches. This supervision shapes current-frame features; it does not provide executed future observations to the policy.

inference.text: Each replanning cycle runs the world backbone once on clean current-observation tokens and caches per-layer keys and values. The action transformer then performs 20 flow-matching steps against this cache. The robot executes all four actions before receiving a new observation and replanning.

The world backbone remains as an encoder, but future-video tokens, the foresight modules and their fusion MLP are absent. There is no generated-video planner, inverse-dynamics conversion or deployed recurrent CoF memory. The policy predicts commands; physical execution occurs outside the learned model.

equations.explanation: Equations (2)–(3): H denotes current-observation hidden states, g fuses selected depths, and z_k^(tau_k) is a noised future latent. The preceding belief is the inter-step information channel; each step also receives present-observation, language and state conditioning.

equations.expression: x_tau = (1-tau)x + tau*epsilon; v = epsilon-x; L = L_v + L_a + lambda*sum_(k=1)^K w_k E[||v_hat_k-v_k||^2]
equations.explanation: Equations (4)–(5) use flow-matching velocity regression for video, actions and foresight. Here x is a clean action chunk or video latent, epsilon is Gaussian noise, and decreasing w_k discounts farther targets. This is supervised prediction, not a reward or online planning objective.

results.setting: Seven subtask combinations; closed-loop completion predicates; three independent evaluation runs.
results.comparison: AC-DiT: 55.6%, a reported difference of 17.4 percentage points. AnchorVLA: 64.0%, averaged over only six reported subtasks.
results.interpretation: The seven-task comparison favors MobileWAM. Its mean cannot be directly compared with AnchorVLA's six-task mean as a matched nine-point gain. These are simulated executions, not video-quality scores.

results.comparison: Sequential improvements of 3.5 and 4.1 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Both additions improve the aggregate in this sequence. Without a MoE-only condition, the table does not isolate their interaction or establish synergistic effects.

results.comparison: Plain WAM 50.2%; parallel foresight 52.3%; MLP CoF 46.3%.
results.interpretation: Expressive recurrent supervision performs best here. Recurrence alone is insufficient, and changing the foresight architecture also changes capacity, limiting a purely causal interpretation.

results.value: Uniform four-layer taps: 58.2%; Mobile MoE: 58.2% in its respective comparison.
results.comparison: All 30 layer taps: 37.1%. Split action experts: 48.8% with bidirectional attention, 46.9% when manipulation reads locomotion, and 44.6% for the reverse.
results.interpretation: The results favor sparse depth-spanning fusion and a shared action representation over the tested alternatives. They do not independently verify the proposed geometry/semantics explanation or semantic expert roles.

results.metric: Milliseconds per prediction cycle, lower is better
results.comparison: Motus 4,950 ms; LingBot-VA 8,126 ms; reported speedups approximately 5.3× and 8.7×.
results.interpretation: This measures prediction-cycle speed, not control frequency or autonomous onboard operation. Physical deployment uses a remote server with two 80GB A800 GPUs; communication overhead is not itemized.

results.setting: Identical fine-tuning data for both methods; randomized initial conditions within the training distribution; full-task completion required.
results.value: Ta drawer opening: 55%; Tb shelf-to-target: 35%; Tc pick-to-shelf: 25%; Td deposit-and-close: 20%; Te compound sequence: 15%.
results.interpretation: MobileWAM improves all five tasks, but trial counts and uncertainty are absent. The longest task still fails frequently. Gains do not grow monotonically with horizon: the largest absolute margin is 20 percentage points on Ta, versus 15 on Te.

limitations.text: The sensing specification is internally inconsistent. Section 3.1 describes joint positions, velocities and base odometry, whereas Appendix A defines an 18-dimensional state containing goal position, grasp status, object pose and end-effector pose. Without explaining how these quantities are obtained, the claim of no privileged states cannot be verified.

Section 4.1 describes 1,000 demonstrations per subtask with 100 held out; Appendix B instead specifies 1,000 training plus 100 validation trajectories. The exact training split therefore remains unresolved.

The statement that every baseline falls to single-digit success somewhere conflicts with Table 1: neither AC-DiT nor AnchorVLA has a reported single-digit entry. The physical results also do not support the asserted monotonic growth of advantage with task horizon or establish out-of-distribution generalization.

The authors identify localization near workspace limits, collision interference and lack of recovery as prominent failure modes. Their descriptions of improved generated perspective and motion-correlated expert routing are qualitative evidence, not quantitative dynamics validation.

What breaks symmetry between initially cloned experts under a zero-initialized router? Expert-specific stochasticity or another asymmetric mechanism might suffice, but the supplied implementation description does not identify one.

reproduction.text: A faithful implementation requires the specified backbone/VAE/text encoder, asymmetric attention masks, per-layer visual caching, independent noise schedules, differentiable CoF recurrence and dense expert mixing. The exact pretrained checkpoint, full-training step count and numerical flow integrator are not identified in the supplied implementation details.

Reproduction also needs resolved state provenance and demonstration splits, evaluation episode counts and seeds, and real-robot demonstration counts and fine-tuning settings. The paper promises code upon acceptance; this statement does not establish availability.

A focused mechanism test would compare serial transformer CoF with a parameter-matched parallel head using identical data, optimization steps, layer taps and loss weights, then evaluate paired closed-loop initial conditions. A separate state-input audit should determine whether success depends on simulator-provided object or goal information.

reasoning.text: Other mechanisms and Outside quadrants fit the deployment mechanism: foresight is auxiliary supervision, actions read current visual features, and neither joint future/action sampling nor inverse dynamics drives execution. Dual-system is convention-dependent here: the source specifies distinct world and action transformer stacks, but they interact at every layer within an integrated mixture-of-transformers. Without a catalog rule for this architecture, joint training alone cannot settle Dual-system versus One Model. Navigation and inference-efficiency tags are supported. Memory should refer to the training-time future-belief chain, not persistent deployment memory.

discussionQuestions: How much success remains when state conditioning contains only quantities available from the deployed robot's sensors? [E18]
Does serial CoF retain its advantage after matching auxiliary-head capacity and training compute? [E12]
What breaks expert symmetry, and do intervention tests establish locomotion/manipulation specialization beyond routing correlations? [E04, E19]
Would persistent observation history improve recovery more than extending the training-only foresight chain? [E06, E17]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title page, abstract and arXiv footer
evidence.detail: Title, identifier and authors match the catalog; the footer specifies v2 and 6 August 2026, the document date says August 7, and the abstract promises code upon acceptance.
The motivation emphasizes moving viewpoints, multimodal base–arm trajectories and delayed navigation consequences; future prediction is proposed as training supervision.
Defines two-camera observations, language/state conditioning, 13-dimensional actions, four-action chunks, the 30-block width-3072 backbone, frozen VAE/T5 and 384 × 640 composited images.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.3; p. 14, Appendix A, Architecture and Mobile MoE
evidence.detail: The width-1024 action stack interacts layerwise through joint attention. Three cloned FFNs are softly mixed by a zero-initialized router over mean-pooled noisy-action embeddings, without balancing loss.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.4, Eqs. (2)–(3); p. 14, Appendix A, Chain-of-Foresight
evidence.detail: CoF fuses layers 4/12/20/30 and chains independent three-block transformer modules through beliefs, without stop-gradient. Foresight noise shift is 10 versus 5 for main branches.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 3.5; p. 14, Appendix A, Decoupled inference
evidence.detail: Current visual tokens exclude future/action information. Inference caches one current-frame backbone pass, denoises actions for 20 steps and executes four actions; future tokens and CoF are absent.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.6, Eqs. (4)–(5); p. 14, Appendix A, Optimization
evidence.detail: Defines Gaussian interpolation, velocity targets, independent branch timesteps and weighted video/action/CoF losses; CoF coefficient is 0.1 with weights 0.4/0.2/0.1.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.1, Training; p. 14, Appendix A, Optimization
evidence.detail: Reports joint expert fine-tuning, frozen VAE/text encoder, AdamW at 10^-5, batch 256, cosine decay, 5% warmup, bf16 and 5,000-step reduced ablations.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 14, Appendix B
evidence.detail: Seven SetTable combinations use official closed-loop completion predicates and three evaluation runs. Main text describes 100 held out from 1,000 trajectories; Appendix B lists 1,000 training and 100 validation.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 4.2; p. 7, Table 1, all subtask rows and Mean row
evidence.detail: Means are MobileWAM 73.0, AC-DiT 55.6 and AnchorVLA 64.0; AnchorVLA lacks Open Drawer. AC-DiT and AnchorVLA have no reported single-digit subtask, contrary to the prose.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 2, Mean row and component columns
evidence.detail: Plain WAM, added CoF, and subsequently added Mobile MoE score 65.4%, 68.9% and 73.0%; no MoE-only condition is listed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 3, caption and Mean row
evidence.detail: At 5,000 steps, plain WAM scores 50.2%, parallel foresight 52.3%, MLP CoF 46.3% and transformer CoF 58.2%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 4, All 30 layers and Uniform 4 layers rows
evidence.detail: Under reduced training, all-layer fusion scores 37.1% and uniform four-layer fusion scores 58.2%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 6, caption and Mean S.R. row
evidence.detail: MoE scores 58.2%; split action experts score 48.8% bidirectionally, 46.9% with manipulation attending locomotion and 44.6% in the reverse direction.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Deployment efficiency; p. 10, Table 7; p. 16, Appendix C, Platform
evidence.detail: A800 prediction-cycle latencies are 938, 4,950 and 8,126 ms. The approximately 6.5B-parameter physical policy runs remotely on two 80GB A800 GPUs over Wi-Fi.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section 4.4; p. 10, Table 8; pp. 16–17, Appendix C
evidence.detail: Ta–Te success is 55/35/25/20/15% for MobileWAM versus 35/25/10/10/0% for π0.5. Both use identical fine-tuning data; evaluation randomizes within the training distribution and requires complete task success.
Reported failures include localization at workspace boundaries, collisions, absent recovery, rest-pose failures and premature drops.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 14, Appendix A, Architecture
evidence.detail: Main text describes joint/odometry state and claims no privileged states; Appendix A instead defines 18-dimensional conditioning using goal position, grasp indicator, object pose and end-effector pose.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section 4.5; p. 17, Appendix D; p. 18, Appendix E
evidence.detail: The authors qualitatively describe improved generated geometry and routing weights tracking motion phases. Appendix E derives phase labels from base and arm speeds; these descriptions are not independent visual inspection.
